questions.question: 1. What is the value of the base-2 logarithm of 512, i.e. $\log_2(512)$?

explanations.a: Incorrect. The corresponding power of 2 would produce a value smaller than 512.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The corresponding power of 2 would produce a value larger than 512.
explanations.c: Correct. Since $2^9 = 512$, the value of $\log_2(512)$ is 9.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The tenth power of 2 is larger than 512.

questions.question: 2. Around 18 teams made it to the final round of a basketball championship. If the team leaders' names are arranged in ascending order and binary search is applied, what is the maximum number of iterations needed to find a particular team leader?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Binary search eliminates a large portion of the remaining search space after each comparison, so it does not require checking all 18 elements in the worst case.
explanations.b: Correct. With the usual binary-search iteration count, the maximum number of comparisons for 18 elements is $\lfloor\log_2(18)\rfloor + 1 = 5$.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The question asks for a maximum number of iterations, not a minimum number.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The maximum number of iterations for this input size is smaller than six.

questions.question: 3. For a standard binary search on a sorted array of length $N$, what is the worst-case order of the number of iterations needed to determine that an element is not present?

explanations.a: Incorrect. This expression can be one comparison too small under the standard counting convention.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The ceiling alone does not account for the final comparison that may establish that the element is absent.
explanations.c: Incorrect. This expression is not the standard floor-based bound used by the formulation in this experiment.
explanations.d: Correct. Under the stated standard counting convention, the worst-case number of iterations can be expressed as $\lfloor\log_2(N)\rfloor + 1$.

questions.question: 4. In the best case, if we perform an optimized linear search on a sorted array of length $N$, how many iterations are needed to determine that a searched value is not present when the value is smaller than the first element?

explanations.a: Incorrect. The ordering information allows the search to stop before examining all elements in this case.
explanations.b: Correct. After checking the first element, the algorithm can determine that a smaller target cannot occur later in an ascending sorted array.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The algorithm does not repeatedly halve the search space in this optimized linear-search procedure.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The algorithm does not perform more than $N$ element checks.

questions.question: 5. In an unsorted array, why can a standard linear search require $N$ comparisons in the worst case?

answers.a: Because the array must first be sorted
answers.b: Because the search examines only the middle element
answers.c: Because every element is always examined twice
answers.d: Because the desired value may be the last element or may not exist

explanations.a: Incorrect. Linear search does not require the array to be sorted.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Linear search checks elements sequentially rather than restricting the search to the middle.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A standard linear search does not need to inspect every element twice.
explanations.d: Correct. If the value is at the last position or absent, the search may need to inspect all $N$ elements.

questions.question: 6. Consider the unsorted array $A = [14, 3, 21, 8, 5]$. Using linear search from left to right, how many elements must be examined to find the value 8?

explanations.a: Incorrect. The value 8 occurs after the first two elements in the given traversal order.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Three elements have been examined only up to the value 21.
explanations.c: Correct. The search examines 14, 3, 21, and then 8, so four elements are examined.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The search stops as soon as 8 is found and does not need to examine 5.

questions.question: 7. Suppose an unsorted array contains $N$ elements and a value is known to occur somewhere in the array. What is the worst-case time complexity of finding its position using linear search?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Knowing that the value exists does not reveal its position.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Linear search does not systematically reduce the remaining candidates by a constant factor.
explanations.c: Correct. The value may occur at the last position, requiring inspection of all $N$ elements.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A single sequential search requires at most a linear number of comparisons.

questions.question: 8. An unsorted array is searched for a value using linear search. If the value is found at the first position, what is the time complexity of the search in the best case?

explanations.a: Correct. Only the first element needs to be examined, so the amount of work is constant.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Examining every element is associated with the worst case, not the best case described here.
explanations.c: Incorrect. No logarithmic reduction of the search space occurs in this best-case scenario.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A single successful comparison does not require quadratic work.

questions.question: 9. Why can binary search be faster than linear search on a sorted array?

answers.a: Binary search always uses more memory
answers.b: Binary search removes approximately half of the remaining search space after each comparison
answers.c: Binary search checks every element simultaneously
answers.d: Binary search does not require the array to be ordered

explanations.a: Incorrect. Memory usage is not the reason binary search reduces the number of comparisons.
explanations.b: Correct. Binary search uses the ordering of the array to discard roughly half of the remaining candidates after each comparison.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Binary search does not inspect all elements simultaneously.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Standard binary search depends on the array being sorted.
